A_target.statement: The three [[Definition:Altitude of Triangle|altitudes]] of a [[Definition:Triangle (Geometry)|triangle]] are [[Definition:Concurrent Lines|concurrent]].

B_source.statement: The three [[Definition:Perpendicular Bisector|perpendicular bisectors]] of the sides of a triangle are concurrent, at its [[Definition:Circumcenter|circumcenter]].

substitutions.the triangle ABC: the larger triangle A'B'C' formed by lines through each vertex parallel to the opposite side

object_map.reformulation: Enlarge the triangle so that its altitudes become perpendicular bisectors of a bigger triangle.

validity_conditions: The parallelograms formed make each original vertex the midpoint of a side of the enlarged triangle.
Perpendicularity to a side is preserved by passing to a parallel side.
proof_plan: Through $A$, $B$, $C$ draw lines parallel to $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively, forming $\triangle A'B'C'$ with $A$ on $B'C'$, $B$ on $C'A'$ and $C$ on $A'B'$.

$ABCB'$ and $ACBC'$ are [[Definition:Parallelogram|parallelograms]], so $AB' = BC = AC'$.
Hence $A$ is the midpoint of $B'C'$, and similarly $B$, $C$ are the midpoints of $C'A'$, $A'B'$.

The altitude from $A$ is perpendicular to $BC$, hence to the parallel line $B'C'$, and passes through its midpoint $A$.
So it is the perpendicular bisector of $B'C'$, and likewise for the other altitudes.
